entries.evidence: The agent critic that ran this round is the installed plugin copy, version 6.14.65, whose tools line reads 'tools: Read, Grep' (/Users/account/.claude/plugins/cache/robotijn/ctoc/6.14.65/agents/pipeline/agent-critic.md, line 4). The repository copy, at VERSION 6.14.69, reads 'tools: Read, Grep, WebSearch, WebFetch'. So the critic could not research the web itself: the citation validator (installed 6.14.65 copy, which holds web tools) did the research under dispatch d-s3-agent-r1-research, and the critic, dispatch d-s3-agent-r1-critic, critiqued against that report. entries.evidence: The applied output format (critic finding f-s3-agent-r1-4) tells the agent to return 'tokens_used: null  # not measurable from inside this agent; never estimate it'. The dispatch schema, .ctoc/architecture/dispatch-schema.yaml line 134, types that field 'tokens_used: { type: integer, minimum: 0 }', and line 132 makes it required. So the honest value the file now orders does not satisfy the schema's type. Nothing breaks today: the only source file that names that schema, src/lib/v8-dispatcher.js, is listed as unreachable in .ctoc/reachability-baseline.json, and every fence that reads the agent file passed after the edit. Two other agents (agents/coordinator/ivv-chief.md line 187, agents/coordinator/synthesizer.md line 215) show 'tokens_used: <int>'. The executor applied the proposal exactly, as ordered, and did not change it; which side moves is a change to a machine-read contract and belongs to the human.

options.label: Keep the agent's null and widen the schema so tokens_used may be null when an agent cannot measure it
options.pros: The agent never reports a number it did not measure (Operating Lesson 18); the same rule can then apply to every agent that cannot see its own token count.
options.cons: A change to the dispatch schema, outside this slice's files, needing its own approved change; any future reader that sums tokens must handle null.

options.label: Change the agent's instruction so it emits an integer, as the schema and two coordinator agents show
options.pros: The agent's response matches the schema as written, with no schema change.
options.cons: An agent cannot read its own token count, so any integer it writes is an estimate or a placeholder presented as a measurement; that reverses a line the critic added for honesty.

entries.evidence: The French Cybersecurity Agency and the German Federal Office for Information Security, joint report "AI Coding Assistants" (https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/KI/ANSSI_BSI_AI_Coding_Assistants.pdf, last updated September 2024), page 8, read by the executor from the saved copy: "There are further risks, such as potential licensing violations when using AI-generated code, which have no direct security connection and are not addressed in the following." No agent's description claims to detect licensed code reproduced into a change: agents/compliance/license-scanner.md line 3 describes it as scanning dependencies for license compliance. The report gives no detection method. The agent critic (dispatch d-s3-agent-r3-critic, finding f-s3-agent-r3-9) proposed no text change: routing it to license-scanner would be a hand-on that agent's description does not claim, and adding a class to this agent would need a method no source gives. Filling the gap would change a file outside this slice (license-scanner or a new agent), so it is put to the human as a scheduling decision.

options.label: Leave licensing of reproduced code unowned for now; the reviewer does not report it
options.pros: No change outside this slice; no detection rule is invented without a source.
options.cons: Licensed code copied into a change by an assistant is checked by no agent; the regulator names the risk.

options.label: Schedule a change that widens license-scanner to cover licensed code reproduced into a change
options.pros: The topic goes to the agent whose domain is licensing; one owner.
options.cons: Needs its own plan, research into a detection method, and a change to license-scanner's description and body.

options.label: Have this reviewer record suspected reproduced licensed code with the words "no owning agent", as it does for files left open
options.pros: The gap becomes visible in every review without choosing an owner yet.
options.cons: A further change to this agent file in a later round or slice; with no method, what counts as suspected stays a reviewer's judgement.

entries.evidence: Google's engineering practices guide, what to look for in a code review (https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/looking-for.html, read 2026-09-30, by the citation validator under dispatch d-s3-skill-r2-research): "In general, tests should be added in the same CL as the production code unless the CL is handling an emergency." The reviewer checks tests that exist (vacuous tests, tests changed to pass) but not a change that adds production code with no tests at all; neither the agent's ten classes nor its hand-on list carries that case. The agent critic (dispatch d-s3-skill-r2-critic, finding f-s3-skill-r2-15) proposed no text: adding it is a scope decision. It named coverage-enforcer as the likely owner, since agents/testing/coverage-enforcer.md line 3 names diff coverage and patch coverage. Giving the case to coverage-enforcer, or adding it as an eleventh class here, changes files outside this slice or this agent's contract, so it is the human's call. Round 3 of the skill (dispatch d-s3-skill-r3-critic, finding f-s3-skill-r3-19) adds regulator support: the joint report "AI Coding Assistants" of the French Cybersecurity Agency and the German Federal Office for Information Security (https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/KI/ANSSI_BSI_AI_Coding_Assistants.pdf, printed page 9, read 2026-09-30) lists among its mitigations "Automatic function tests should be employed."

options.label: Leave a change that adds no tests unchecked by this reviewer
options.pros: No change to the reviewer's ten classes or to another agent.
options.cons: Assistant-written production code that arrives with no tests is flagged by no class of this reviewer.

options.label: Have this reviewer record such a change for coverage-enforcer, and schedule coverage-enforcer to own it
options.pros: The check goes to the agent whose description already names diff and patch coverage.
options.cons: A change to this agent's hand-on list and to coverage-enforcer, in a later slice or plan.

options.label: Add "change adds no tests" as an eleventh class of this reviewer
options.pros: Visible in every review of assistant-written code with no new owner needed.
options.cons: Widens this agent's contract and output types; needs its own change to the agent file, its skill and possibly the dispatch type list.

entries.evidence: The agent needs Bash to query a registry and read the status code, so a package name taken from untrusted code can reach a shell. Round 1 added a character check the agent performs itself, single quotes, and a second check inside each recipe; all three are instructions, nothing enforces them, and the second check cannot catch a single quote. tests/watcher-shape.test.js lines 94-100 call Bash "a write tool wearing a read tool's coat". The only enforcement point would be the Bash pre-tool hook, src/hooks/PreToolUse.Bash.js, which is outside this slice. This is a decision on how much risk to accept. The Step 13 security review (dispatch d-s4-step13-secure, Info 3) adds the general point: the agent's read-only use of Bash is itself an instruction, not a fence; the grant is unrestricted, and a command the shell-write coverage check cannot identify as a write is not stopped by it.

options.label: Keep the check at the instruction level as written
options.pros: No change outside this slice; the session's live run saw every hostile name tried refused.
options.cons: Nothing stops an agent that skips its own check; a name holding a line break followed by the recipe's end marker is guarded only by that check (a single quote is now read as text and refused by the recipe's own check).

options.label: Add a guard in the Bash pre-tool hook that refuses this agent's commands when a registry address holds characters outside the allowlist
options.pros: The rule holds even when the agent does not follow it.
options.cons: A change to a security hook, which needs its own approved plan; the hook must be able to tell which agent is running, which was not checked.

entries.evidence: Round 2 added a rule for a private-looking name that the public registry answers with status 200: the agent records it as a possible dependency confusion, with "no owning agent named here", and never treats REGISTERED as settling it (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts threat model, https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.1/threats: "Register a package name in a public registry that shadows a name used on the victim's internal registry"). Settling it would mean querying the organisation's own private registry, which needs a recipe, credentials and a scope this agent was never given. Whether to give it those is a decision about risk and scope.

options.label: Keep the agent recording a possible dependency confusion, with no private-registry access
options.pros: No credentials reach an agent that handles untrusted names in a shell; nothing outside this file changes.
options.cons: A shadowed private name is never settled by this agent; someone must check it by hand or with another tool.

options.label: Give the agent a read-only recipe and credentials for the organisation's private registry
options.pros: The agent can compare the public and private answers and settle the case itself.
options.cons: Puts registry credentials in reach of an agent whose inputs are untrusted; needs a credential-handling design and its own approved change.

entries.evidence: Round 3 made the npm recipe print whether the latest version carries provenance (provenance=present) or was published through trusted publishing (trusted_publisher=yes), read from https://registry.npmjs.org/<name>. The agent can report that provenance is present; it cannot report that it is valid, because verifying a signature needs a tool its grant (Read, Grep, Bash) does not hold, and the file forbids reporting provenance as verified. The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity's draft advisory on artificial-intelligence-assisted software development (version 0.4, table 5) says "Where available, verify package signing, integrity or provenance metadata." Whether to add verification, and at what cost, is a decision about risk.

options.label: Keep the agent reading only whether provenance is present
options.pros: No new tool or dependency; the file already says provenance is never reported as verified.
options.cons: A package with forged or mismatched provenance reads the same as one with valid provenance.

options.label: Give the agent a way to verify provenance signatures
options.pros: The agent could tell valid provenance from present provenance.
options.cons: Needs a verification tool or dependency and a change to the agent's tool grant, which the plan keeps fixed; its own approved change.

entries.evidence: The skill's "Tool Integration (2026)" section recommends a gate for continuous integration built from third-party tools (Socket, Snyk, Aikido, cosign, OpenSSF Scorecard, deps.dev, Dependency-Track, slopcheck). The wrapper agent never runs that gate and tells the agent never to cite it ("Read the method first", item 4), and several of those tools' claims were not checked in round 1 (finding f-s4-skill-r1-27). Round 1 made the gate safe to read (names first, no lifecycle scripts) but did not decide whether the skill should keep it. That is a scope decision.

options.label: Keep the recommended gate in the skill, checked further in later rounds
options.pros: Readers keep a worked example of a pipeline gate; round 1 already removed its unsafe order.
options.cons: The skill carries tool claims its own agent never uses, each needing sources in every round.

options.label: Remove the gate section from the skill and keep only the wrapper's read-only recipes
options.pros: The skill describes only what its agent does; fewer unchecked tool claims.
options.cons: Loses the pipeline guidance; the pinned headings "Tool Integration (2026)" are quoted by the wrapper and would need a coordinated edit.

entries.evidence: Round 3 limits the LOW triage tier for a renamed library: the page for technique T1195.001 (https://www.cisa.gov/eviction-strategies-tool/info-attack/T1195.001, carrying the same words as https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/001/, both read 2026-09-30) says a supply-chain compromise "may also include abandoned packages, which in some cases could be re-registered by threat actors after being removed by adversaries". The rule triages a renamed library as LOW only when the registry answer shows the maintainers the well-known project has. Only the wrapper's npm recipe prints maintainers ("The PyPI, crates.io and Maven Central recipes print none of these", agents/ai-quality/hallucination-detector.md), so, applied strictly, no renamed library outside npm could ever be LOW. The files now keep LOW where the recipe prints no maintainers, with "maintainers not read" in the limitations; the same scoping is in the wrapper's renamed_package severity row (late correction). Which rule to keep is a decision about how much risk to accept. The Step 11 review (dispatch d-s4-step11-review, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-step11-review-d-s4-step11-review.md, item 7) adds the npm case: when an npm answer carries no maintainers, the recipe prints maintainers="not in the answer" and both files then treat the name as suspected_lookalike (high), while the same missing data on PyPI keeps LOW. The npm answer without maintainers is therefore handled the opposite way to PyPI. The renamed rule now also reads "shares at least one maintainer with" the well-known project, because the session's probe found react-query and @tanstack/react-query share one maintainer but not all (.ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-agent-round3-session-runs.md).

options.label: Keep the rule as written: LOW where the registry's recipe prints no maintainers (PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central); an npm answer without maintainers counts as a mismatch, so suspected_lookalike (high)
options.pros: npm, whose recipe can read maintainers, gets the stricter reading when they are missing.
options.cons: Missing maintainers mean high on npm and low elsewhere.

options.label: Keep LOW wherever maintainers were not read, npm answers without maintainers included, with "maintainers not read" in the limitations
options.pros: One rule for missing data on every registry.
options.cons: A re-registered name on npm whose answer omits maintainers is triaged LOW.

options.label: Triage a renamed library as LOW only when maintainers were read and at least one is shared; otherwise suspected_lookalike, on every registry
options.pros: A re-registered abandoned name is never triaged LOW without evidence of a shared owner.
options.cons: Every renamed library outside npm becomes suspected_lookalike, severity high.

entries.evidence: Round 3 of skills/ai-quality/hallucination-detector/SKILL.md now says react-codeshift was "created 2026-01-14 by a third party, maintainer \"debugducky\" ... That is not a registry hold: the wrapper's npm recipe prints REGISTERED for it" (https://registry.npmjs.org/react-codeshift, read 2026-09-30). The finished reviewer skill, skills/ai-quality/ai-code-quality-reviewer/SKILL.md line 184, calls it "a defensive placeholder"; its own line 176 already says an Aikido researcher registered the name. entries.evidence: The Step 13 security review (dispatch d-s4-step13-secure, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-step13-secure-d-s4-step13-secure.md, Low 5): every package name the wrapper checks is sent to public services (npm, PyPI, crates.io, Maven Central, and npm's downloads interface) before the private-name rule is applied, and the skill's gate runs `socket ci`, which uploads the manifests to a third party. A client's internal package names can therefore leave the approved data boundary. The user-agent string names only the public repository. Which way to go is a decision about data boundaries.

options.label: Keep querying every name, internal-looking ones included
options.pros: Dependency-confusion detection keeps the public answer it needs.
options.cons: Client-internal names reach npm, PyPI and Socket.

options.label: Hold back names the private-name rule matches unless the dispatch says the data boundary allows sending them
options.pros: Nothing internal leaves the boundary without permission.
options.cons: Dependency-confusion detection is lost for exactly those names.

entries.evidence: The citation validator's re-read after the kickbacks (dispatch d-s4-post-kickback-revalidate, .ctoc/audit/improvement-run-notes/s4-post-kickback-revalidate-d-s4-post-kickback-revalidate.md, "Leads") found two things the PyPI recipe does not read. PyPI's JSON answer carries owner roles: sklearn has "ownership":{"organization":null,"roles":[{"role":"Owner","user":"filo"},…]} (https://pypi.org/pypi/sklearn/json, read 2026-09-30), so the recipe could print owners and let the shared-maintainer rule apply to PyPI instead of writing "maintainers not read". And PyPI's index interface serves a project-status object with "active", "archived" or "quarantined" (https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2025-08-14-project-status-markers/, read 2026-09-30); a status marker is not a hold. Either would change what the recipe prints, which is a design decision.

options.label: Extend the PyPI recipe to print owners (and the status marker) and apply the shared-maintainer rule to PyPI
options.pros: A renamed PyPI library can be triaged on the same evidence as npm; a quarantined or archived project is visible.
options.cons: New recipe code, a session run, and a re-validation; the status marker comes from a second interface and a second request per name.

options.label: Leave the PyPI recipe as it is, with "maintainers not read" in the limitations
options.pros: No new code; the limitation is stated in every report.
options.cons: PyPI renamed libraries keep the weaker evidence, and a quarantined project reads the same as an active one.

entries.evidence: Both files hand "C and C++ language issues" to sast-scanner (wrapper hand-on list; skill C and C++ section). Which sibling owns C and C++ issues that are not about security is an ownership decision.

options.pros: One pointer, already consistent in both files.
options.cons: Memory-safety issues that are not security findings point to an agent whose scope is security.

options.cons: Two pointers to keep in step across both files; a text change in both.
